lead: The fluid slowed inside a boundary layer carries less mass, less momentum and less energy than the same height of free-stream fluid. Rather than compare whole velocity profiles, engineers squeeze each deficit into one length in metres: displacement thickness δ*, momentum thickness θ and energy thickness δ<sub>E</sub>. These lengths turn a complicated profile into three numbers. They feed wall-shear formulas, drag estimates and boundary-layer control. A pipeline designer or a wing analyst uses them to answer: how much does this layer thicken the body, and how much drag or energy loss does it cause?
prereq: You need: 5.1 for the boundary layer and the velocity profile u(y) inside it.

blocks.text: Inside the layer the velocity u rises from 0 at the wall to the free-stream value U. Take y as height above the wall and δ as the boundary-layer thickness where u ≈ U. The same height of free-stream fluid would carry more mass, more momentum and more kinetic energy. Each deficit is written as the free-stream value multiplied by a length.

blocks.where: u is the local velocity in m/s at height y in m; U is the free-stream velocity in m/s; δ is the boundary-layer thickness in m; δ* is the displacement thickness in m.

blocks.text: δ* is the height by which the wall would have to move outward to give the same mass-flow deficit. The missing mass flow per unit width is ρUδ*, with ρ the density in kg/m³. It is a fictitious distance, not the visible edge of the layer.

blocks.where: θ is the momentum thickness in m; other symbols are as above. The missing momentum flux per unit width is ρU²θ.

blocks.text: θ is the height of free-stream fluid whose momentum equals the momentum lost by the slow layer. It is the key length in drag calculations because wall shear feeds momentum loss.

blocks.where: δ<sub>E</sub> is the energy thickness in m; some syllabi write δ** for it. The missing kinetic-energy flux per unit width is (1/2)ρU³δ<sub>E</sub>.

blocks.text: The shape factor H = δ*/θ is a dimensionless number. A profile that stays slow over most of the layer (laminar) has a large mass deficit compared with its momentum deficit, so H is high. A fuller profile near the wall, as in turbulent flow, has lower H. For the Blasius laminar layer on a flat plate, δ*/δ ≈ 0.34, θ/δ ≈ 0.13 and H ≈ 2.59.
For a straight-line profile u/U = y/δ, put η = y/δ. Then dy = δ dη and η runs from 0 to 1. The three integrals become simple polynomials.
δ* = δ∫₀¹(1 − η)dη = δ/2; θ = δ∫₀¹ η(1 − η)dη = δ/6; δ<sub>E</sub> = δ∫₀¹ η(1 − η²)dη = δ/4
blocks.where: η is the dimensionless height y/δ; the results are in metres when δ is in metres.

blocks.text: For the 1/7 power law u/U = η^(1/7), used as a rough model of a turbulent layer, the integrals give δ* = δ/8, θ = 7δ/72 ≈ 0.0972δ and δ<sub>E</sub> = 7δ/40 = 0.175δ. Then H = (δ/8)/(7δ/72) = 9/7 ≈ 1.29. A real turbulent layer has H around 1.3 to 1.4, so the simple power law is reasonable but not exact.

The momentum integral equation links θ to the shear stress at the wall τ<sub>w</sub> in N/m². For a flat plate with zero pressure gradient, τ<sub>w</sub> = ρU² dθ/dx, where x is distance along the plate in m. The derivative dθ/dx has units of m/m = dimensionless, so the right side has units kg/m³ × m²/s² = kg/(m·s²) = N/m².

This equation is useful because θ grows along the plate as the layer thickens. Measure or compute θ(x), differentiate it, and you get τw(x) without finding the slope of the velocity profile at the wall. Integrate τw over the plate area and you get the friction drag. That step is in 5.4.

When pressure changes along the surface, an extra term appears; the simple form above is for a flat plate at zero pressure gradient. For the straight-line profile example, θ = δ/6, so if δ grows with x, τ<sub>w</sub> is proportional to dδ/dx.

figure.caption: A linear velocity profile branches into the three thickness definitions. The numbers are the fractions of δ for u/U = y/δ, and the shape factor is H = 3.

spec.aria: One velocity profile branching into the three thickness definitions with their values for a linear profile, and the shape factor H equal to 3.

examples.question: A boundary layer of thickness δ = 10 mm has the straight-line profile u/U = y/δ. Find δ*, θ, δ<sub>E</sub> and H.
steps: δ* = ∫ from y = 0 to 10 mm of (1 − y/10) dy = [y − y²/20] from 0 to 10 = 10 − 5 = 5.0 mm.
δ<sub>E</sub> = ∫ from y = 0 to 10 mm of (y/10)(1 − y²/100) dy = [y²/20 − y⁴/4000] from 0 to 10 = 5 − 2.5 = 2.5 mm.
examples.answer: δ* = 5.0 mm, θ = 1.67 mm, δ<sub>E</sub> = 2.5 mm and H = 3.0.
examples.check:
delta = 10.0
ds = delta / 2
theta = delta / 6
de = delta / 4
H = ds / theta
print(round(ds, 2))
print(round(theta, 2))
print(round(de, 2))
print(round(H, 2))

traps: Do not write H = θ/δ*. The shape factor is H = δ*/θ, dimensionless, and is greater than 1 for a real layer.

Energy thickness uses (u/U)(1 − (u/U)²), not (1 − u/U). For the linear profile this gives 0.5δ instead of 0.25δ, exactly twice too large; for the 1/7 power law it gives 0.125δ instead of 0.175δ. Either way the number is wrong, so use the correct integrand.
δ* is not the same as δ. δ is where u reaches U; δ* is a fictitious extra wall distance. Keep all three thicknesses in metres.
Integrate up to y = δ, or beyond where u = U, and use the free-stream U in every ratio. Stopping at an arbitrary height leaves part of the deficit uncounted.
All three integrands are positive because u ≤ U. A negative thickness means u/U was inverted or the limits were swapped.

quiz.a: δ* = ∫₀^δ (1 − u/U) dy. It is the fictitious outward shift of the wall that gives the same mass-flow deficit as the real layer, in metres.

quiz.q: Write the energy thickness integral and say what δ** means.
quiz.a: δ<sub>E</sub> = ∫₀^δ (u/U)(1 − (u/U)²) dy. Some syllabi write δ** for the same energy thickness.
It is one dimensionless number that describes profile shape. High H means a slow, weak layer with a large mass deficit; low H means a fuller profile. Blasius laminar H ≈ 2.59; 1/7 power law H ≈ 1.29.

quiz.q: A linear profile has δ = 20 mm. Find θ.
A 1/7 power-law layer has δ = 14 mm. Find δ*, θ and H.
Same δ, linear versus 1/7 profile: which H is higher and why?
quiz.a: Linear H = 3, power law H = 1.29. The linear profile keeps u low over most of the layer, so the mass deficit δ* is large compared with momentum deficit θ. The 1/7 profile rises faster near the wall, reducing δ*.

quiz.q: For ρ = 1000 kg/m³, U = 2 m/s and dθ/dx = 0.002, find τ<sub>w</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. Integral boundary-layer methods such as Thwaites' method use θ and H to predict growth without solving the full Navier–Stokes equations. CFD reports δ*, θ and H because they summarise a profile in three numbers. Transition and drag-reduction studies track θ growth; riblets and plasma actuators aim to reduce it. Search: momentum integral equation, shape factor boundary layer, Thwaites method, energy thickness.
